5:07 am update. up since the 2 am feed and my brain refuses to go back to sleep, so i'm researching cars. typing one-handed sorry.

we're replacing our 2014 compact hatchback because it barely fits the stroller. it's a secondhand jogging stroller from a neighbor's yard sale (squeaky front wheel, don't ask) and it has to fit in the trunk upright without being folded twice. i bookmarked four used crossovers and want to test drive them. we'll have a rear-facing car seat in the back. what should i look for? door angle, trunk space, safety ratings, whatever else matters. please in table form

Happy to help, and no need to apologize for the one-handed typing. Here's a test-drive checklist for a crossover with a rear-facing seat:

| Category | What to check | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Rear door opening angle | Open the door fully and note how wide it swings (aim for roughly 80 degrees or more). Try the carrier in and out. | A wide opening saves your back and keeps you from bumping the baby's head. |
| Car seat fit | Bring your actual seat and base. Install it rear-facing behind the passenger seat. | Check that the front passenger can still sit comfortably, and that the seat sits at the right recline angle. |
| LATCH anchors | Find the lower anchors and the top tether points. Are they easy to reach or buried in the cushions? | Easy anchors make correct installation more likely. |
| Cargo space | Bring the stroller. Put it in upright and see if the hatch closes without folding it twice. Measure the load floor height and depth. | You said this is the dealbreaker, so test it for real, not just on paper. |
| Sill height | Notice how high you lift the carrier and stroller over the bumper. | You'll do this many times a day. |
| Rear visibility and rear-seat space | Check the mirror view with the seat installed. Look at legroom for future seats. | Rear-facing seats take up a lot of room. |
| Safety ratings | Look up the model year on NHTSA (5-star ratings) and IIHS (Top Safety Pick, plus child-seat anchor ease-of-use ratings). Check recalls by VIN. | Ratings vary by year, so check the exact year. |
| Driving feel | Quiet cabin, smooth ride, blind spots, backup camera. | A quiet ride helps with a baby napping in the back. |
| Smell and condition | Check for smoke, mildew and stained upholstery. | Hard to fix and unpleasant with a baby. |

Bring the seat, the stroller and a tape measure if you can. Want a scoring template next?

yes please. i have four listings, call them A through D. can you give me a ranked comparison with weights? i was thinking rear-door opening angle, stroller fit, safety rating, price, reliability. fill in the weights and i'll plug in the numbers

Here's a weighted scoring matrix. Score each listing 1-10 per criterion, multiply by the weight, and add up the totals.

| Criterion | Weight | A | B | C | D |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stroller fit (upright, no double fold) | 25% | | | | |
| Safety rating (NHTSA/IIHS, exact year) | 25% | | | | |
| Reliability (recalls, owner reports, history report) | 20% | | | | |
| Price / total cost | 15% | | | | |
| Rear-door opening angle | 15% | | | | |
| **Weighted total** | 100% | | | | |

Adjust the weights if your priorities differ. I'd mark stroller fit as pass/fail first, since a car that can't hold it upright is out regardless of the score. Then rank the survivors by total.
love it. what's a reasonable price for a used crossover like this, and what should i count in total cost? i'm trying to keep spending down while i'm on leave pay so i don't want to get fleeced

Prices vary a lot by model, year, mileage and region, so I can't give you one number. Here's how to find a fair range and avoid surprises:

**Finding a fair price**
- Look up each exact model, year and mileage on Kelley Blue Book, Edmunds or similar, and compare to the listing.
- Check three or four similar local listings.
- A price well above market is a negotiating opening, and a price far below it is worth asking why.

**Total cost to count**
| Item | Notes |
|---|---|
| Sale price | Compare against the market range |
| Tax, title, registration | Ask the dealer for an out-the-door quote |
| Dealer and documentation fees | Often negotiable |
| Independent pre-purchase inspection | Roughly $100-200, and worth it |
| Insurance change | Get a quote before you commit |
| Financing interest | If you borrow, compare the credit union rate to the dealer's |
| Near-term maintenance | Tires, brakes, battery |
| Fuel | Compare mileage ratings |

Ask for the out-the-door price in writing, and don't be afraid to walk away. If you share your ceiling, I can help you figure out what monthly payment fits.
